1.23 Instability of Trees
Decision trees are interpretable, but they can also be unstable.
A small change in the dataset may lead to:
• a different root split,
• different thresholds,
• a different overall tree structure.

Example: A small change, a different first question
Suppose in the triage data the two best root candidates are symptom severity and age,
with nearly identical impurity reduction. If one borderline patient is added, removed, or
relabeled, the preferred root split may change from severity to age. The whole downstream
tree may then change as well.
Interpretability should not be confused with robustness. A tree can be easy to read and
still be sensitive to small changes in the data.
1.24 Axis-Parallel Limitation
A standard decision tree usually splits on one attribute at a time:

• the model is easy to explain,
• the tests are simple,
• mixed data are handled naturally.
But it also has a limitation:
• some class boundaries are diagonal, curved, or interaction-based, and cannot be represented
compactly with only one-variable splits.

1.25 Practical Do’s and Don’ts
Do’s
• Define the object, attributes, and class label precisely.
• Check that predictors are available at the moment of prediction.
• Respect attribute type when defining split conditions.
• Preserve order when splitting ordinal variables.

• Ask whether a split is conceptually meaningful, not only numerically attractive.
• Interpret a leaf as a local class distribution, not only as a hard label.
• Be suspicious of identifiers and near-identifiers.
• Ask what missing values mean before deciding how to handle them.
• Remember that unseen categories can occur in practice.
• Treat a learned tree as one possible model, not as the unique truth.
Don’ts
• Do not think that a classification problem is well defined just because a dataset has a column
that could be used as a label.
• Do not assume that every variable stored in the dataset is automatically a legitimate
predictor.
• Do not believe that a split is useful only because it produces very pure child nodes on the
training data.
• Do not interpret a learned threshold as if it were automatically a scientific or domain-specific
law.
• Do not treat a tree as if it were the unique or final explanation hidden in the data.

• Do not read a leaf label as if it expressed absolute certainty; always remember that it comes
from the local class composition of the training data.
• Do not assume that missing values are harmless technical nuisances; they may reflect part
of the real process that generated the data.
• Do not expect a one-variable-at-a-time split to capture every important interaction present
in the data.
• Do not judge a classifier only by how easy it is to read; interpretability and reliability are
not the same thing.
1.26 Summary
Classification is the supervised task of learning a mapping from attributes to predefined class
labels. But a good classification analysis begins before the model is trained. It begins with a
careful definition of the object, the label, the decision moment, and the set of predictors that are
genuinely available.
Decision trees are an especially useful first model because they represent classification as a
sequence of explicit tests. They make it easy to see how induction works, how a record is
classified, how different attribute types lead to different split conditions, and how impurity
measures guide the choice of splits.
The core material remains essential: the distinction between training and prediction, the recursive
idea of Hunt’s algorithm, the role of binary, nominal, ordinal, and continuous attributes, and the
use of Gini, entropy, information gain, and gain ratio to compare candidate splits.

At the same time, real classification

material remains essential: the distinction between training and prediction, the recursive
idea of Hunt’s algorithm, the role of binary, nominal, ordinal, and continuous attributes, and the
use of Gini, entropy, information gain, and gain ratio to compare candidate splits.

At the same time, real classification practice requires more than formulas. A classifier only learns
the label that has been defined. Predictors must be available at prediction time. Not every
impurity-reducing split is meaningful. Leaves store local class evidence, not only class names.
Missing values and unseen categories are normal practical issues. Trees are interpretable but can
be unstable, and their standard split geometry is axis-parallel.
Thus, the real lesson of basic classification is not only how to build a tree. It is how to think
correctly about what the label means, what information is legitimate, what a split actually says,
and when a mathematically attractive classifier may still be the wrong one for the problem.

1 Errors, Overfitting, and Model Evaluation in Classification
1.1 Introduction
A classification model is built to make predictions on records that were not used during training.
Because of this, the central question in classification is not whether a model fits the training
data well, but whether it generalizes well to unseen data.
In the previous lecture we asked whether the predictors and splits were meaningful. Now we ask
whether a tree that looks reasonable on the training data will still work well on unseen data.
In practice, a model may achieve very small error on the training set and still perform poorly
on new observations. This gap between apparent performance and true predictive performance
is one of the main reasons why model evaluation and model selection are essential topics in
classification.
Decision trees provide a particularly clear setting for studying these ideas. A tree can be made
very small and simple, or it can be grown into a highly detailed structure with many nodes.
As the tree becomes more complex, training error typically decreases. However, this does not
guarantee that test error will also decrease.
This chapter studies the basic types of classification errors, explains how overfitting arises, and
presents principled ways to select, simplify, and evaluate models.

1.2 Classification Errors
When evaluating a classifier, several notions of error must be distinguished.
Definition: Training error
The training error (also called apparent error) is the error committed by the classifier on
the same training records that were used to build the model.
Definition: Test error
The test error is the error committed by the classifier on a separate test set that was not
used during model training.
Definition: Generalization error
The generalization error is the expected prediction error of the model on new records
drawn from the same underlying distribution as the training data.
Training error is easy to compute, but it is usually optimistic. Test error is more informative,
provided the test set has not influenced model building. Generalization error is the ideal quantity
of interest, but it is typically unknown and must be estimated indirectly.
Remark: Why these three errors differ?
A classifier is optimized to perform well on the training set. Therefore training error is
often lower than test error. Generalization error is broader still: it refers not only to one
fixed test set, but to future data sampled from the same population.
Insight: Test error is an estimate, not the target quantity itself
Test error is an estimate of generalization error, not the generalization error itself.
They are often reasonably close when:
• the test set is large enough;
• the test set is representative of the target population;
• the test data come from the same distribution as future data;
• the test set is not reused during tuning or repeated model revisions;
• there is no leakage, that is, no unintended flow of test or future information into the
training process.

• the test set is not reused during tuning or repeated model revisions;
• there is no leakage, that is, no unintended flow of test or future information into the

They can differ substantially when the test set is small or biased, when future data come
from a different population, when the same test set is inspected many times during tuning,
or when the data are very noisy or highly variable.
There are different ways to define the error that we will measure. We can use the misclassification
error, as we will do for simplicity for the rest of the chapter. But we can also use some of the
known measures as accuracy, F1 score, precision etc, which we will introduce in the next sections.
Example: A simple interpretation
Suppose a classifier is trained on 200 student records and evaluated on 100 unseen student
records.
• If it misclassifies 10 of the 200 training cases, the training error is 10/200 = 0.05.
• If it misclassifies 18 of the 100 unseen cases, the test error is 18/100 = 0.18.

The difference between these values suggests that the classifier may not generalize as well
as the training error alone would indicate.

1.4 Underfitting and Overfitting
Definition: Underfitting
A model is said to underfit when it is too simple to capture the important structure in the
data. In this case, both training error and test error are typically large.
Definition: Overfitting
A model is said to overfit when it is too complex and starts fitting accidental patterns,
noise, or peculiarities of the training set. In this case, training error may be small while
test error is large.
Underfitting and overfitting are opposite failures:
• An underfit model has not learned enough.
• An overfit model has learned too much from the particular training sample, including aspects
that do not generalize.

Insight: Central practical principle
As model complexity increases, training error often decreases monotonically. Test error
does not have to do so. This is the essence of overfitting.

1.5 Effect of Training Set Size
One of the simplest and most important observations in machine learning is that larger training
sets often reduce overfitting.
When more training data are available:
• the model sees a broader sample of the population;
• accidental peculiarities have less influence;
• the difference between training error and test error often becomes smaller.
A highly complex model may still overfit, but the same model complexity is usually less dangerous
when the dataset is much larger.

At a fixed model complexity, increasing the size of the training set often reduces the gap

1.6 Why Overfitting Happens
Two major reasons for overfitting are especially important in classification:
• limited training size;
• high model complexity.
A further subtle issue is the multiple-comparison effect, which appears whenever a learning
algorithm searches through many candidate model components and keeps whichever one appears
best.
Definition: Model complexity
Model complexity refers to the expressive flexibility of the model. For decision trees,
complexity increases with quantities such as depth, number of internal nodes, number of
leaves, and the fineness of the induced partition.
1.6.1 The Multiple-Comparison Effect
Suppose many candidate variables, thresholds, or test conditions are examined. Even if none of
them carries real signal, some may look useful by chance on the training set.
This means that an algorithm can overfit not only because it is flexible, but also because it is
given many opportunities to discover spurious improvements.
Example: Stock prediction analogy
Suppose a person makes random guesses about whether the stock market will go up or
down over 10 days. The probability of getting at least 8 out of 10 guesses correct by chance
is not very large for one individual. But if 50 people each guess randomly, the probability
that at least one of them appears remarkably successful becomes much higher (almost 1).
If we then select the “best” person, we may wrongly believe we found skill, when in fact
we only found chance.
Insight: Why this matters for learning algorithms?
Many learning algorithms use a greedy rule of the form:
M′ = M ∪ γ,
where γ is a candidate component to add to the model, such as a split in a decision tree.
If γ is chosen from a large set of alternatives, some irrelevant component may seem

If γ is chosen from a large set of alternatives, some irrelevant component may seem helpful
purely by chance and may be added, increasing overfitting risk.
Example: Noisy variables
Suppose a two-dimensional classification task can already be solved well using variables X
and Y . If we now add 100 completely noisy variables and allow a decision tree to search
over all of them, some of those noisy variables may look useful on the training data. This
can lead to a more complex tree and worse test performance.

Warning: A practical lesson
The presence of many irrelevant or noisy variables increases the risk that a greedy algorithm
will discover accidental improvements and build an unnecessarily large model.
Remark: A practical workflow when many noisy variables are present
If there are many noisy variables, a decision tree may split on them by chance and overfit.
Therefore, one should control complexity with pruning and penalties, and choose tree size
using validation or cross-validation rather than training error alone.
A practical interpretation is:
• Before building: remove variables that are obviously irrelevant, duplicated, leaky, or
meaningless for prediction, when domain knowledge and data inspection justify this.
• While building: use pre-pruning or stopping rules so that weak accidental improve-
ments do not create unnecessary nodes.
• After building: use post-pruning to remove subtrees that do not improve estimated
generalization.
• For selection: compare candidate tree sizes using a validation set or cross-validation
instead of relying on training error alone.

1.7 Why Training Error Is Not Enough?
Training error usually decreases when a model becomes more flexible. For this reason, it is an
optimistic measure of performance. It tells us how well the model has fit the seen data, not how
well it will perform on unseen records.
Definition: Optimistic estimate
An estimate of model performance is called optimistic if it tends to report better perfor-
mance than the model actually achieves on new data.
Remark: Training error as an optimistic estimate
Resubstitution error, that is, error measured on the training data, is often optimistic
because the same data were used both to build and to evaluate the model.
This is why model selection requires methods for estimating generalization error rather than
simply minimizing training error.
1.8 Model Selection
Definition: Model selection
Model selection is the process of choosing among alternative models or model sizes during
training, with the goal of obtaining good generalization rather than merely low training
error.
The purpose of model selection is to avoid choosing a model that is more complex than necessary.
In decision trees, this often means determining whether a node should be split, whether a subtree
should be retained, or whether the tree should be pruned.
Three general approaches are especially important:
1. using a validation set;
2. incorporating model complexity directly;

3. estimating statistical bounds on error.
Algorithm: What quantity is actually compared during pruning?
When deciding whether to keep a split, keep a subtree, or prune it away, what we actually
compare is an estimated generalization error. This estimate can be obtained in several
ways.
1. Validation-set estimate. Build candidate trees, or candidate pruned versions of a
tree, on a

deciding whether to keep a split, keep a subtree, or prune it away, what we actually
compare is an estimated generalization error. This estimate can be obtained in several
ways.
1. Validation-set estimate. Build candidate trees, or candidate pruned versions of a
tree, on a training subset and compare them on a validation subset. Then keep the
version with lower validation error or better validation performance.
2. Complexity-penalized estimate. Use a criterion of the form
training error + penalty for complexity.
For decision trees, this becomes the pessimistic error estimate, where larger trees or
trees with more leaves receive a larger penalty.
3. Statistical upper bound on error. Instead of only adding a direct complexity
penalty, adjust the observed error upward to reflect uncertainty, especially when leaves
are small. Then compare the parent node with its children, or compare a full subtree
with its pruned version, using those upper bounds.
Thus, pruning decisions should not be based on training error alone; they should be based
on whichever estimate of out-of-sample performance the chosen procedure uses.
1.8.1 Model Selection Using a Validation Set
A standard strategy is to divide the available training data into two parts:
• a training subset, used to build the model;
• a validation subset, used to estimate generalization error and choose model complexity.
Definition: Validation set
A validation set is a subset of the available training data that is reserved for model selection,
hyperparameter tuning, or early stopping. It is different from the final test set.
This approach is conceptually simple and often effective. Its drawback is that it reduces the
amount of data available for fitting the model itself.
Warning: Validation set versus test set

Warning: Validation set versus test set
The validation set is used during model building. The test set is not. If the test set

1.8.2 Incorporating Model Complexity
Another approach is to evaluate a model by combining its training fit with a penalty for complexity.
This reflects the principle known as Occam’s Razor.
Definition: Occam’s Razor in model selection
If two models achieve similar predictive performance, the simpler model is generally
preferred because it is less likely to have fitted accidental structure.
A generic penalized criterion can be written as
Estimated Generalization Error = Training Error + λ · Complexity(Model),

where λ is a trade-off parameter.
The intuition is simple:
• good fit is desirable;
• complexity is risky;
• model selection balances the two.
Insight: Interpretation of the penalty term
A complexity penalty does not assume that all complex models are bad. Instead, it says
that a complex model should justify its complexity by improving enough to offset its added
risk.

1.10 Pruning Decision Trees
Pruning is the process of simplifying a decision tree so that it generalizes better.
There are two broad approaches:
• pre-pruning;
• post-pruning.
1.10.1 Pre-Pruning
Definition: Pre-pruning
Pre-pruning stops tree growth early, before the tree becomes fully developed.
Typical stopping rules include:
• stop if all instances at a node belong to the same class;
• stop if all attribute values are the same;
• stop if the number of instances is below a user-defined threshold;
• stop if the class distribution appears independent

stopping rules include:
• stop if all instances at a node belong to the same class;
• stop if all attribute values are the same;
• stop if the number of instances is below a user-defined threshold;
• stop if the class distribution appears independent of the candidate features;
• stop if impurity does not improve enough;

• stop if estimated generalization error no longer improves.
Remark: Advantage and risk of pre-pruning
Pre-pruning can prevent overfitting and reduce computation, but if used too aggressively
it may stop the tree before important structure is discovered.
1.10.2 Post-Pruning
Definition: Post-pruning
Post-pruning first grows the tree more fully and then removes subtrees whose presence
does not improve generalization.
Two common ideas are:
• subtree replacement: replace a subtree by a single leaf if this improves the estimated
generalization error;
• subtree raising: replace a subtree with one of its branches when this yields a simpler and
better tree.
Example: Subtree replacement
Suppose a node contains 30 training records with majority class Yes. If replacing the
whole subtree by a single leaf gives a pessimistic error estimate of 10.5/30, while keeping
the split gives 11/30, then the subtree should be pruned.
Warning: Do not confuse lower training error with better tree
A subtree may slightly reduce training error and still be undesirable if it increases estimated
generalization error.

1.11 Model Evaluation
Model selection and model evaluation are related but not identical.
Definition: Model evaluation
Model evaluation is the process of estimating how well a classifier performs on previously
unseen data.
The main goal is to estimate predictive performance honestly.

1.11.1 Holdout Method
Definition: Holdout method
In the holdout method, the available data are partitioned into a training set and a test set.
The classifier is trained on the former and evaluated on the latter.
For example, one may reserve 70% of the data for training and 30% for testing.
Remark: Repeated holdout
Instead of performing one random split only once, one may repeat the holdout procedure
several times with different random splits. This is called repeated holdout or random
subsampling.
The holdout method is simple and easy to implement, but its estimate may be unstable if the
dataset is small or if the particular split is not representative.
1.11.2 Cross-Validation
Definition: k-fold cross-validation
In k-fold cross-validation, the data are partitioned into k disjoint subsets (folds). The
model is trained k times, each time using k − 1 folds for training and the remaining fold
for testing.
The final estimate is usually the average of the k test errors.
Special cases include:
• leave-one-out cross-validation: k = n, so each observation serves as a test point once;
• repeated cross-validation: perform cross-validation multiple times with different fold
assignments;
• stratified cross-validation: preserve class proportions in each fold (important for imbal-
anced classes).

Definition: Stratified cross-validation
Stratified cross-validation preserves approximately the same class proportions in each fold
as in the full dataset.
This is especially important when:
• the classes are imbalanced;

• the sample size is small.
Definition: Nested cross-validation
Nested cross-validation uses an inner cross-validation loop for model selection and an outer
cross-validation loop for final performance evaluation.
Nested cross-validation is particularly important when model selection is substantial, because it
prevents optimistic bias from tuning and testing on effectively the same data.
Warning: Cross-validation misuse
If hyperparameters are chosen using the same folds that are then reported as final perfor-
mance, the resulting estimate may be too optimistic. Nested cross-validation is designed
to avoid this.
Warning: Preprocessing leakage inside evaluation.
If scaling, imputation, encoding, or feature selection is performed on the full dataset before
cross-validation, the evaluation may become optimistically biased. Such preprocessing
steps must be fitted using only the training portion of each split or fold, and then applied
to the corresponding validation or test portion.
Remark: Default settings are only generic starting points
Default tree settings are chosen by a software library for broad usability, not for your exact
sample size, noise level, class imbalance, or real prediction goal. Therefore, leaving them
unchanged can easily produce an overgrown or misleading tree.
In practice, the algorithm and the data scientist have different roles:
• the algorithm provides a rule for searching candidate splits and building candidate
trees;
• the data scientist must decide how complexity will be controlled, which evaluation
metric matters, and how model selection and performance estimation will be

and the data scientist have different roles:
• the algorithm provides a rule for searching candidate splits and building candidate
trees;
• the data scientist must decide how complexity will be controlled, which evaluation
metric matters, and how model selection and performance estimation will be carried
out.
A good practical workflow is to treat the defaults only as a baseline, then adapt stopping
rules, minimum leaf size, maximum depth, pruning strength, and evaluation metric to
the problem using validation or cross-validation. This is especially important for small
or imbalanced datasets, where one should control depth and leaf size more carefully and
should not rely only on training accuracy.
1.12 Practical Do’s and Don’ts
Do’s
• Distinguish clearly among training, validation, and test performance.
• Expect training error to be optimistic.
• Use validation sets or cross-validation for model selection.
• Prefer simpler models when their performance is comparable.
• Use pruning or other regularization to control decision-tree complexity.
• Use stratified cross-validation for imbalanced data.
• Use nested cross-validation when both tuning and evaluation are important.

• Treat default tree settings as baselines, not as final problem-specific decisions.
• Choose the evaluation metric to match the task; for example, in screening problems sensitiv-
ity/recall may matter more than raw accuracy.
Don’ts
• Do not choose the model solely because it has the smallest training error.
• Do not confuse a validation set with a test set.
• Do not report performance from a test set that influenced model design.
• Do not interpret very deep trees as automatically better.
• Do not ignore the role of noisy variables and multiple comparisons.
• Do not assume that a single random split is always reliable.
• Do not assume that a library default is automatically appropriate for your sample size, class
imbalance,

Insight: A robust guiding principle
A good classifier is not the one that explains the training set most perfectly. It is the one
that predicts unseen data most reliably.
1.13 Summary
Training error, test error, and generalization error are distinct concepts, and confusing them leads
to poor conclusions. A classifier may perform very well on the training set while still generalizing
poorly.
Overfitting occurs when a model becomes too complex and begins to fit accidental patterns in
the training data. Underfitting occurs when the model is too simple to capture the relevant
structure. In decision trees, these ideas are especially visible because increasing the number of
nodes almost always lowers training error, while test error may eventually increase.
Overfitting is encouraged by limited training size, excessive model complexity, and multiple
comparisons among many candidate variables or model components. Good model selection
therefore requires more than minimizing training error.
Three main strategies were exist:
• using a validation set;
• penalizing model complexity;
• using statistical bounds on error (it is not discussed here).
For decision trees, these ideas lead naturally to pre-pruning and post-pruning. Finally, honest
performance assessment requires proper evaluation procedures such as holdout, cross-validation,
stratified cross-validation, repeated cross-validation, and nested cross-validation.
In practice, one should also remember that default library settings are only generic starting points.
The data scientist must choose a suitable complexity control strategy, a suitable evaluation
protocol, and a suitable performance metric for the actual problem.

1 Ensemble Methods and Boosted Trees for Classification
1.1 From a Single Tree to an Ensemble
In the previous lectures, decision trees were introduced as intuitive classification models: they
partition the feature space through a sequence of split conditions and produce a class decision at
the leaves. They are attractive because they are easy to read, easy to visualize, and naturally
handle nonlinear interactions.
But the previous lectures also established three important ideas:
• a model should be judged by its performance on unseen data, not by training fit alone;
• classifier quality depends on the practical goal, the class distribution, and the consequences

and naturally
handle nonlinear interactions.
But the previous lectures also established three important ideas:
• a model should be judged by its performance on unseen data, not by training fit alone;
• classifier quality depends on the practical goal, the class distribution, and the consequences
of errors;

• a tree that looks convincing on one sample may change noticeably if the sample changes.
Next we want to understand what happens when many trees are combined into one stronger
classifier.
Insight 1.1: Why this is the natural next step?
A single tree is often attractive because of interpretability, but it may be unstable and
may overfit. Ensemble methods are a natural continuation because they try to keep the
flexibility of tree-based learning while improving stability and predictive performance.
1.2 Why Single Trees Can Be Unstable?
A decision tree is built greedily: at each node, the algorithm searches for a split that looks best
according to some impurity criterion such as entropy, Gini index, or misclassification error. Small
changes in the training data may change which split looks best. Once an early split changes, the
whole lower part of the tree may change as well.
Definition 1.1: Decision tree instability
A decision tree is called unstable if small perturbations in the training data can produce a
noticeably different fitted tree and therefore different predictions.
Example 1.1: Medical triage threshold instability
Suppose a hospital uses a decision tree at triage to classify patients into Urgent
respiratory condition versus Non-urgent other condition. If one or two patients
close to a threshold on oxygen saturation or symptom severity are added, removed, or
corrected, the first split of the tree may change. Then the entire diagnostic structure below
that split may change as well.
This instability is closely related to the bias-variance tradeoff. A shallow tree

a threshold on oxygen saturation or symptom severity are added, removed, or
corrected, the first split of the tree may change. Then the entire diagnostic structure below
that split may change as well.
This instability is closely related to the bias-variance tradeoff. A shallow tree is often too simple
and may have high bias. A very deep tree may capture detailed local structure, but it may also
become too sensitive to accidental patterns in the training data, which leads to high variance.
Definition 1.2: Bias-variance tradeoff
The bias-variance tradeoff describes two competing sources of prediction error:
• bias: error that occurs when a model is too rigid or too simple to capture the true
underlying pattern in the data well. Such a model makes restrictive assumptions and
can systematically produce inaccurate predictions.
• variance: error that occurs when a model depends too strongly on the particular
training sample. In that case, small changes in the training data can lead to a
noticeably different fitted model and different predictions.
A good model should be flexible enough to capture the real structure in the data, but
stable enough that small changes in the training sample do not lead to large changes in
prediction.
Remark 1.1: Why this matters?
Instability is not automatically bad. In fact, it becomes useful in ensemble learning. If
different training perturbations produce different trees, then those trees may make different
errors, and combining them can improve generalization.

1.3 The General Idea of Ensemble Learning
An ensemble combines multiple base models into one final predictor. For classification, the
combination is often made by majority vote or by aggregating scores or probabilities.
When the base learners are trees, two broad ensemble philosophies dominate:
1. Bagging: build many trees independently on perturbed versions of the training data and
aggregate their predictions.

When the base learners are trees, two broad ensemble philosophies dominate:
1. Bagging: build many trees independently on perturbed versions of the training data and
aggregate their predictions.
2. Boosting: build trees sequentially so that each new tree improves what the current ensemble
is still getting wrong.
Definition 1.3: Ensemble method
An ensemble method is a learning strategy that combines several base models into one
final predictor, usually to improve stability, robustness, or predictive accuracy.
Remark 1.2: Two fundamentally different ideas
Although bagging and boosting both combine many trees, they should not be treated as
the same idea:
• bagging mainly reduces variance through averaging;
• boosting mainly improves predictive fit through sequential correction.
1.4 Bagging: Averaging Many Trees
1.4.1 Bootstrap sampling
Bagging begins with the bootstrap. A bootstrap sample is obtained by sampling, with replacement,
from the training set until one again has a sample of the same nominal size.
Definition 1.4: Bootstrap sample
Given a dataset of size n, a bootstrap sample is obtained by drawing n observations
with replacement from the original dataset.
Sampling with replacement means that after an observation is drawn, it is placed back and can
be drawn again. Thus one bootstrap sample may contain repeated copies of some observations,
while others may not appear at all. This repetition is not an error; it is the central mechanism of
the bootstrap.

Bootstrap resampling is a way to mimic repeated sampling from the population by using

Remark 1.3: What bootstrap resampling means in practice?
Bootstrap resampling is a way to mimic repeated sampling from the population by using
the observed dataset as an empirical stand-in for that population. If a train/validation/test

split already exists, bootstrap resampling is applied to the training set, while the validation
and test sets remain untouched.
Warning 1.1: Bootstrap is not a universal fix
Bootstrap resampling does not automatically preserve every important structure. If the
data are time-dependent, clustered, severely imbalanced, or already contaminated by
leakage, then ordinary bootstrap may reproduce the wrong structure. The resampling unit
must match the data-generating structure. (In such cases, one uses adapted resampling
schemes, such as block bootstrap for time-dependent data, cluster-level resampling for
grouped data, or stratified resampling when class proportions must be preserved.)

1.4.3 Why bagging works?
Bagging is most effective when the base learner is unstable. Different bootstrap samples produce
somewhat different trees. If those trees do not make exactly the same errors, averaging or voting
can reduce the net effect of sample-specific noise.

Insight 1.2: Bagging as variance reduction
Bagging is best understood as a variance-reduction method. It does not try to learn one
perfect tree. Instead, it averages many unstable trees so that random fluctuations of

Remark 1.4: Why the correlation of errors matters?

1.4.4 What bagging does and does not do?
Bagging can improve predictive stability, but it does not solve every problem.
• It does not repair data leakage.
• It does not guarantee interpretability.
• It does not eliminate the need for validation.

1.5 Out-of-Bag Error
When a tree is trained on a bootstrap sample, not every training observation is selected into that
sample. The observations that are left out can still be used in a useful way: they act like a small
temporary test set for that particular tree. These omitted observations are called out-of-bag
observations.
Definition 1.5: Out-of-bag observation
For a given bootstrap sample, an observation is out-of-bag if it was not included in that
sample.
Now consider one training observation. Some trees were trained using it, but some trees did not
see it at all because it was out-of-bag for them. We can therefore predict its class using only the
trees that did not use it during training. If we do this for all training observations and compare
the aggregated predictions to the true classes, we obtain the out-of-bag error.
Remark 1.5: Why OOB is useful?
Out-of-bag error is especially useful in bagging and Random

trees that did not use it during training. If we do this for all training observations and compare
the aggregated predictions to the true classes, we obtain the out-of-bag error.
Remark 1.5: Why OOB is useful?
Out-of-bag error is especially useful in bagging and Random Forest because it provides a
built-in estimate of predictive performance as part of the training procedure itself. This
allows evaluation without creating an extra validation split inside the training data, and
often with less computational cost than repeated cross-validation.

Warning 1.2: What OOB does not replace?
Out-of-bag error is helpful, but it does not replace a final untouched test set. Final model
assessment should still be based on honest evaluation on data not used in model building.
1.6 Random Forest
1.6.1 Why plain bagging is not always enough?
If every bagged tree sees all features at every split, many trees may become too similar, especially
when one variable is very dominant. In that case, averaging many similar trees brings less benefit
than averaging more diverse trees.
1.6.2 The Random Forest idea
Random Forest extends bagging by adding feature randomness. Each tree is trained on a
bootstrap sample, but at each split the algorithm considers only a random subset of candidate
features.
Definition 1.6: Random Forest
A Random Forest is an ensemble of decision trees in which:
• each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of the data;
• each split is chosen from a random subset of features rather than from all features;
• final prediction is obtained by majority vote in classification.
This produces two sources of randomness:
• observation-level randomness through bootstrapping;
• feature-level randomness through random candidate subsets.
The purpose of the second source is to reduce correlation among the trees, so that averaging
becomes more effective. Here, and in the

• observation-level randomness through bootstrapping;
• feature-level randomness through random candidate subsets.
The purpose of the second source is to reduce correlation among the trees, so that averaging
becomes more effective. Here, and in the rest of the lecture notes, "averaging" does not mean
averaging the trees themselves. It means averaging the predictions they produce, such as class
scores or estimated probabilities. If the trees output only class labels, the ensemble prediction is
usually obtained by majority vote.

Example 1.3: Medical triage and dominant variables
Suppose oxygen saturation is by far the strongest triage variable. Under plain bagging,
many trees may repeatedly split first on that same variable. Under Random Forest, some
trees are forced to consider other variables such as respiratory rate, reported symptom
severity, or patient age. This increases diversity across trees and may improve the ensemble.
Remark 1.6: Interpretation of Random Forest
Random Forest is often the first strong ensemble baseline in practice because it is: accurate
on many tabular datasets, relatively robust, less sensitive to tuning than many boosted
methods, naturally suited to nonlinear interactions.
At the same time, Random Forests are less transparent than a single tree, and feature importance
measures require careful interpretation, especially in the presence of correlated variables.
Remark 1.7: Transparency and

methods, naturally suited to nonlinear interactions.
At the same time, Random Forests are less transparent than a single tree, and feature importance
measures require careful interpretation, especially in the presence of correlated variables.
Remark 1.7: Transparency and feature importance in Random Forests
A single decision tree is transparent because one can literally read its splits from top to
bottom and explain a prediction as a path such as “if age > 50 and cholesterol > 220, then
class = risk.” A Random Forest is an average of many trees, often hundreds, so there is no
single simple path that represents the whole model. This usually improves prediction, but
it reduces interpretability.
Feature importance also requires care. In a Random Forest, an important variable is
usually one that helps prediction a lot across the ensemble. But this becomes tricky when
variables are correlated. For example, suppose both age and years_since_retirement
carry almost the same information. The forest may use one of them in some trees and
the other in other trees. Then the apparent importance may be split between them, or
one may look unimportant only because its correlated partner was chosen first. Thus,
“low importance” does not always mean “no information,” and “high importance” does not
always mean “unique causal role.”
1.7 Measuring Feature Importance
Because we cannot trace a single decision path in a Random Forest, feature importance is usually
assessed by measuring how much each variable contributes to the predictive performance of the
ensemble. Two common methods are:
• Impurity-based importance (Gini importance): This sums the reduction in node
impurity (such as the Gini index or entropy) achieved by a feature across all trees. It is fast
to compute, but it can be misleading when predictors are highly correlated or

common methods are:
• Impurity-based importance (Gini importance): This sums the reduction in node
impurity (such as the Gini index or entropy) achieved by a feature across all trees. It is fast
to compute, but it can be misleading when predictors are highly correlated or when some
variables have many possible split points or many categories.
• Permutation importance: This measures how much predictive performance worsens when
the values of one feature are randomly shuffled in validation, test, or out-of-bag data. A
large drop in performance suggests that the model relied strongly on that feature.
When predictors are strongly correlated, feature importance should be interpreted with caution,
because correlated variables may share predictive information. In such cases, it is often useful to
examine correlated features together, or to use grouped permutation importance, rather than
assuming that one variable alone carries the entire importance.

1.8 Boosting: Sequential Error Correction
Bagging builds trees independently and then aggregates them. Boosting is fundamentally different.
It builds trees one after another, and each new tree is chosen specifically to improve the current
ensemble.
Definition 1.7: Boosting
Boosting is an ensemble strategy in which base learners are added sequentially, each one
chosen to improve the performance of the current ensemble.
The core idea is:
Do not try to learn one perfect tree. Learn a sequence of small trees, where each new
tree corrects part of what the current ensemble still gets wrong.

tree with only one split.

Insight 1.3: AdaBoost versus bagging
Bagging builds many trees independently and stabilizes prediction by aggregation. Ad-
aBoost builds learners sequentially and changes the observation weights from round to
round so that later learners focus more on cases that were previously misclassified.
Warning 1.3: A practical caution
Because AdaBoost repeatedly increases the influence of observations that were misclassified
in earlier rounds, it can over-focus on mislabeled cases, outliers, or strong noise. In such
situations, the algorithm may keep trying to correct observations that should not be fitted
closely, which can hurt generalization. This sensitivity is a general property of the method.
In modern tabular-data applications, AdaBoost is often less preferred, because stronger
and more flexible boosted-tree methods are available.

In binary classification, gradient boosting usually models a score function F(x) rather than a

Remark 1.12: Choosing the number of boosting rounds
There is no universal fixed number of boosting iterations that is best for all problems. In
practice, one usually chooses the number of rounds by validation or cross-validation. The
model is trained for many rounds, but performance is monitored on separate validation
data, and one stops at the iteration where validation performance is best. This is called
early stopping.
The number of boosting rounds and the learning rate must be chosen together: a smaller
learning rate usually requires more iterations, while a larger learning rate often requires
fewer.

2.4 LightGBM
LightGBM is designed with computational speed and large-scale learning in mind. Two ideas are
especially important for understanding it:
• histogram-based splitting: continuous feature values are grouped into bins, which makes
split search much faster;
• leaf-wise tree growth: instead of growing all leaves level by level, the algorithm extends
the leaf that currently looks most promising.
Remark 2.2: How to think about LightGBM
The key practical message is speed and scalability. LightGBM is especially attractive when
the dataset is large and fast experimentation matters.
These design choices can make LightGBM very efficient, especially on large tabular datasets. At
the same time, leaf-wise growth can produce more aggressive trees, so the method may need
careful control of depth, leaf size, and regularization.
Typical strengths include:
• fast training;
• strong performance on large tabular datasets;
• efficient handling of many features.
Typical cautions include:
• aggressive tree growth can overfit if not controlled;
• hyperparameters controlling tree size and regularization matter strongly;

• speed does not remove the need for proper evaluation.
2.5 CatBoost
CatBoost is particularly important when categorical variables play a central role. It is designed
to handle categorical information in a more principled way than naive one-hot encoding in many
settings.
A central idea in CatBoost is the use of ordered target statistics. Instead of replacing a category
by a naive target mean computed from the whole dataset, which may create target leakage,
CatBoost uses an ordered scheme that reduces this problem and gives a more careful estimate of
category information.
Remark 2.3: How to think about CatBoost
CatBoost is especially valuable when high-cardinality categorical variables are important,
categories are rare, and careless encoding could create leakage or unstable estimates.
CatBoost is also known for using oblivious (symmetric) trees,

Remark 2.3: How to think about CatBoost
CatBoost is especially valuable when high-cardinality categorical variables are important,
categories are rare, and careless encoding could create leakage or unstable estimates.
CatBoost is also known for using oblivious (symmetric) trees, where all nodes at the same depth
use the same split condition.
Example 2.1: A simple categorical contrast
Suppose an admissions dataset contains a variable high_school_ID with many possible
categories. A naive one-hot encoding may create a large number of binary columns and
may behave poorly if some schools appear only a few times. CatBoost instead tries to
summarize category signal through ordered target statistics, which can be more compact
and often more robust in such situations.
Typical strengths include:
• strong handling of categorical predictors;
• reduced danger of naive target leakage in category encoding;
• good performance on tabular problems where categories are central.
Typical cautions include:
• it is not automatically best on every dataset;
• careful validation and tuning are still needed;
• interpretability issues remain similar to those of other boosted-tree systems.
Insight 2.1: Main takeaway of this section
XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost are all boosted-tree systems built on the same general
idea. Their practical differences come mainly from design priorities: XGBoost emphasizes
robust regularized boosting, LightGBM emphasizes speed and scalability, and CatBoost
emphasizes principled handling of categorical variables.
2.6 Practical Hyperparameters and Their Meaning
Although software packages differ, the most important conceptual hyperparameters are similar
across modern boosted-tree systems.

• Number of trees / boosting rounds. More trees increase expressive power, because the
model can make more correction steps. But too many trees may overfit, especially if the
learning rate is large or the individual trees are too complex.
• Learning rate. The learning rate controls how strongly each

boosting rounds. More trees increase expressive power, because the
model can make more correction steps. But too many trees may overfit, especially if the
learning rate is large or the individual trees are too complex.
• Learning rate. The learning rate controls how strongly each new tree changes the current
score function. Smaller learning rates usually require more boosting rounds, but they often
give a more gradual and stable fit.
• Tree depth or number of leaves. These parameters control the complexity of each
individual tree. Shallow trees produce simpler corrections, while deeper trees or larger
numbers of leaves can capture richer interactions but may overfit more easily.
• Subsampling. Using only a subset of rows or columns at each boosting round can regularize
the model and reduce variance.
• Regularization parameters. Modern implementations often include penalties or con-
straints that discourage overly complex trees or overly large leaf values.
Remark 2.4: Three high-impact hyperparameters
Among the most influential tuning parameters in boosted trees are:
• the number of trees,
• the learning rate,
• the complexity of each tree.
These parameters interact strongly and should usually be tuned together rather than one
by one in isolation.
Remark 2.5: A practical view of fine-tuning
Fine-tuning should usually begin with the three high-impact hyperparameters above.
A smaller learning rate often requires more trees. Larger or deeper trees often require
stronger regularization or fewer rounds. In practice, tuning is usually done with validation
or cross-validation, often together with early stopping, rather than by trying to optimize
one parameter at a time on the test set.

2.7 Practical Do’s and Don’ts for Modern Boosted Tree Systems
Do’s
• Begin with a simpler baseline before moving to a more elaborate boosted system.
• Use validation, cross-validation, and early stopping whenever possible.
• Tune the learning rate, number of trees, and tree complexity jointly.
• Check carefully how categorical variables are handled in the chosen implementation.
• Interpret feature importance as predictive importance, not as causal importance.
Don’ts
• Do not judge model quality from training error alone.
• Do not tune hyperparameters on the test set.

• Do not assume that a modern library automatically removes the need for careful preprocessing
and validation.
• Do not treat one package as universally best for every tabular dataset.
• Do not ignore leakage, mislabeled data, or unstable category encoding.
XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost are all members of the same boosted-tree family. Their main
differences are practical rather than conceptual in the deepest sense. XGBoost emphasizes robust
regularized boosting, LightGBM emphasizes speed and scalability, and CatBoost emphasizes
principled handling of categorical variables.
For practical use, you should remember that the most important tuning decisions usually concern
the number of trees, the learning rate, and the complexity of the individual trees. These choices
interact strongly and should be made with validation rather than by trial and error on the test
set.

2.9 Summary
A single decision tree is attractive because it is easy to interpret, but it may be unstable and
sensitive to the particular training sample. Ensemble methods address this weakness in two main
ways.
Bagging and Random Forest mainly reduce variance by aggregating many trees. Random Forest
strengthens this idea by forcing more diversity through feature randomness. Boosting is different:
it builds trees sequentially so that each new tree improves the current ensemble. AdaBoost

emphasizes harder cases through reweighting, while gradient boosting fits correction trees to a
loss-based error signal.
Modern systems such as XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost are all boosted-tree systems built
on that same general idea, but with different practical design priorities. Their choice depends
less on abstract theory alone and more on issues such as regularization, computational scale, and
handling of categorical variables.
The main practical lesson of this lecture is that powerful ensemble methods are not automatic
solutions. Their performance depends on thoughtful

Remark. Memoryless property
A probability distribution is said to be memoryless if the probability of an event occurring in the future
is independent of the past. In other words, the distribution ”forgets” how much time has already elapsed.
More specific, given that the event has not yet occurred by time s, the probability of waiting at least t
additional time units is the same as it was at the beginning. Mathematically, if X is a random variable
with the memoryless property, then for any s,t ≥ 0:
P(X > s + t

occurred by time s, the probability of waiting at least t
additional time units is the same as it was at the beginning. Mathematically, if X is a random variable
with the memoryless property, then for any s,t ≥ 0:
P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).
This equation means that, regardless of how long you have already waited (time s), the probability
that you will need to wait at least an additional t units of time is the same as the probability of waiting
at least t units of time from the start.
The Exponential distribution is the only continuous distribution with this property (and the Geometric
distribution is its discrete counterpart).
Example 3.3. Memoryless property Suppose X represents the waiting time (in minutes) for an elevator,
and X follows an Exponential distribution with rate λ. Then, no matter how long you have already waited,

the probability that you must wait at least an additional 5 minutes is always:
P(X > s + 5 | X > s) = P(X > 5) = e−5λ.
This illustrates the memoryless property of the Exponential distribution. □
Remark. Exponential distribution can be generalised with Weibull and Gamma distribution. See also

3.13 How to analyze heavy tailed distributions
When dealing with heavy-tailed distributions (Pareto, Cauchy and other distributions), the tail may be so
heavy that the mean and/or the variance may be infinite. Thus many standard statistical measures and
tests can not be applied.

- In this cases mean and standard deviation can not be used to describe the data. We have to choose
measures which are less influenced by extreme values as median, quantiles, trimmed means, median absolute
deviation (MAD) etc.
- Many standard statistical methods are based on means and variances (Central limit theorem, confidence
intervals, estimators especially with method of moments, parametric tests etc.). This methods can not be
used when mean and variance

as median, quantiles, trimmed means, median absolute
deviation (MAD) etc.
- Many standard statistical methods are based on means and variances (Central limit theorem, confidence
intervals, estimators especially with method of moments, parametric tests etc.). This methods can not be
used when mean and variance are infinite or nonexistant. Alternative methods should be used, specifically
designed for analysis of heavy tails. This part of statistics is called extreme value theory. One example
is Hill estimator for the parameter α in Pareto distribution - we can focus on analysis of the tail and the
extreme values.
- Logarithmic transformations, when suitable, can transform the data and decrease the extreme values,
they can reveal some structures and some standards methods may be aplicable.
- Also we should consider some non-parametric and simulation methods. (Discuss Kurtosis)
3.14 Bimodal distributions are their analyzes
A bimodal distribution is a probability distribution with two distinct local maxima (modes) in its
probability density function (PDF) or frequency histogram. These two peaks often suggest that the data
may be drawn from two different underlying subpopulations or processes.
Characteristics
• Two Peaks - the defining feature is the presence of two separate modes;
• Heterogeneity: Bimodality often indicates that the dataset comprises two groups with different char-
acteristics;
• Variability - depending on the separation and height of the peaks, the overall spread and shape of
the distribution may differ from standard unimodal distributions.
• Skewness and kurtosis - the individual modes may have different skewness or kurtosis properties.
What are we allowed to do?
• We can use histograms or kernel density estimates to visually inspect the data for bimodality;
• If bimodality is observed, explore whether it reflects genuine subgroups in the data. Domain knowl-
edge is important;
• We can use mixture models (e.g., Gaussian mixture

• We can use histograms or kernel density estimates to visually inspect the data for bimodality;
• If bimodality is observed, explore whether it reflects genuine subgroups in the data. Domain knowl-
edge is important;
• We can use mixture models (e.g., Gaussian mixture models) to formally model the two components.
• When we want to summarize central tendency, we can use more robust statistics and consider medians
or quantiles if outliers or mixed subpopulations are present.
What to be careful about?
• We should not assume normality and we should not automatically apply standard parametric tests
which assume unimodal, symmetric data;
• We should ensure that the observed bimodality is not due to data collection errors or improper
binning,
• There may be an overlap - in cases of slight bimodality, be cautious about splitting the data without
a strong theoretical or empirical justification.

Important Features
• Mode Separation - the distance between the two peaks can provide insights into the degree of het-
erogeneity.
• Relative Peak Heights - differences in peak heights may indicate the relative size or importance of
the subpopulations.
• How the distribution tails behave beyond the modes can be important for risk assessment and extreme
value analysis.
How to analyze bimodal data?
• Graphical Methods - histograms, kernel density plots, and box plots are useful for initial exploration;
• Statistical Tests - formal tests like Hartigan’s Dip Test or Silverman’s Test can be used to assess
multimodality;

4 Families of distributions
Next we present several important families of distributions.
4.1 Exponential family
This is a very broad class of distributions which have a probability density (or mass) functions in a specific
canonical form. Many properties of these distributions, such as the mean, variance, and moment generating

functions etc. can be derived from this form, making it easier to perform analytical calculations. This family
includes many well-known distributions such as Normal (Gaussian), Exponential, Gamma, Bernoulli and
Binomial, Poisson and Beta distributions. In Bayesian context these distributions have so called conjugate
prior and we will use them in the Chapter for Bayesian statistics.
4.2 Location-Scale Family
Distributions in this family can be transformed into one another via linear transformation.

4.2 Location-Scale Family
Distributions in this family can be transformed into one another via linear transformation. This family

4.4 Extreme value distributions
Extreme value distributions arise in the study of the extreme values (maximum or minimum) of large
samples of random variables. More specifically these distributions arise in the study of first and last order
statistics.
The key idea of extreme value theory is that the maximum (or minimum) of a large number of inde-
pendent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables — when properly normalized — will converge in
distribution to one of three types of distributions. Which type of distribution applies depends on the tail
behavior.
Type I Gumbel distribution - The Gumbel distribution typically appears as the limiting distribu-
tion for the maximum of samples drawn from distributions with exponentially decaying tails (light-tailed
distributions), such as the normal or exponential distributions.
Type II Fr ́echet distribution The Fr ́echet distribution arises as the limit for the maximum of samples
from heavy-tailed distributions, such as the Pareto distribution. It is characterized by a power-law decay
in the tail - if we move further into the tail of a probability

Fr ́echet distribution The Fr ́echet distribution arises as the limit for the maximum of samples
from heavy-tailed distributions, such as the Pareto distribution. It is characterized by a power-law decay
in the tail - if we move further into the tail of a probability distribution, the probabilities decrease at a
rate proportional to a power of the variable, i.e. for large x p(x) ∼ Cx−α, where C is a constant α > 0.
Such Power-law tails are observed in many real-world phenomena - we have observed already the case
for wealth distribution. Another examples are
• Earthquake Magnitudes: Larger earthquakes, while rare, occur more frequently than would be pre-
dicted by exponential decay;
• Many real networks have many nodes with small degree and a few nodes with extremely large degree.
This can be modeled with a power-law tail:
P(X ≥ k) ∼ Ck−α
which means that the probability that a node has at least k links decays as a power of k. Types
of datasets: a web graph, social network, citation network, GitHub dependency network, Internet
traffic (the number of links on web pages).
• Word Frequencies and Zipf’s Law: In natural language, word frequencies have been observed to follow
a power-law pattern known as Zipf’s law:

The applications are broad:
• Modeling extreme losses and gains (risk management, finance, insurance);
• Modeling extreme weather events (floods, hurricanes) - estimating the probability of very rare events
is important for planning and risk assessment;
• Predicting the failure times of production components which are subject to stress (reliability engi-
neering).
Machine learning with heavy-tailed and extreme-value data. When data contain heavy tails or
extreme values, standard machine learning methods must be used carefully, because models optimized for
average error often describe the center of the distribution well but fail in the tail. In such problems, the
goal is often not only prediction of the mean, but estimation of rare-event probabilities, high quantiles,
exceedance risk, or tail behavior. Standard approaches include log-transformations, robust regression,
quantile regression, anomaly detection methods, and hybrid models that combine machine learning for
covariates with extreme-value models such as GEV or generalized Pareto distributions for the tail.
Important practical issues are tail scarcity and imbalance: extreme observations are rare, so models
may ignore them unless the loss function, sampling strategy, or evaluation metric gives them sufficient
importance. Tail-weighted losses, cost-sensitive learning, oversampling of extreme cases, or separate mod-
eling of exceedances over a

practical issues are tail scarcity and imbalance: extreme observations are rare, so models
may ignore them unless the loss function, sampling strategy, or evaluation metric gives them sufficient
importance. Tail-weighted losses, cost-sensitive learning, oversampling of extreme cases, or separate mod-
eling of exceedances over a threshold are often used. Evaluation should include tail-specific metrics, such as
high-quantile error, exceedance classification accuracy, or calibration of rare-event probabilities, not only
RMSE or overall accuracy.
One should be careful not to treat all extremes as errors or outliers, because in heavy-tailed data
they may be genuine observations. At the same time, individual extremes have high influence, so robust
validation, sensitivity analysis, and comparison with simpler statistical tail models are important. Random
train–test splitting can also be misleading in temporal or spatial extremes; block or time-aware validation
is usually more appropriate.
Clustering and classification with heavy-tailed data. For classification, the main difficulty is that
extreme cases are often rare, so the problem becomes an imbalanced-learning problem. Standard classifiers
may achieve high overall accuracy while missing the rare but important tail events. Therefore, cost-sensitive
classification, class weighting, oversampling of rare events, threshold tuning, anomaly-detection methods,
and evaluation by precision, recall, F1-score, ROC/PR curves, and tail-specific error rates are commonly
used. In some applications, labels are defined through exceedances, for example X > u, and the task
becomes classification of whether an observation belongs to the extreme-risk region.
For clustering, methods such as k-means should be used carefully, because means and Euclidean dis-
tances are strongly affected by extreme observations. More robust alternatives include clustering after
log-transformation, clustering with robust distances, k-medoids instead of k-means, density-based methods
such as DBSCAN/HDBSCAN, or model-based clustering with heavy-tailed distributions such as Student-t

mixtures. In multivariate extreme-value analysis, one may also cluster observations according to their tail
behavior, for example

robust alternatives include clustering after
log-transformation, clustering with robust distances, k-medoids instead of k-means, density-based methods
such as DBSCAN/HDBSCAN, or model-based clustering with heavy-tailed distributions such as Student-t

mixtures. In multivariate extreme-value analysis, one may also cluster observations according to their tail
behavior, for example by grouping observations that become extreme together.
The main warning is not to automatically remove extreme observations as outliers. In this setting, they
may be the most informative part of the data. Instead, one should decide whether the goal is to model the
bulk of the data, the tail, or both separately.
There are different methods for statistical inference when working with extreme value problems. One
of them is block maxima method - the data is devided into blocks and the maximum in each block is
analyzed.
Example 4.3. Extreme flood levels of a river. We can be interested in the annual maximum river
discharge to assess flood risk. We can collect hydrological data - yearly the maximum water level (or
discharge) is recorded. The data can be divided in blocks (here we will use a year as a block) and the
yearly annual maxima can be analyzed with the extreme value theory.
Studies have shown that the Gumbel distribution is often a good model, because river flows typically
have exponentially decaying tails. We have to fit appropriate distribution and then it can be used to
estimate the probability of very high flood levels. Based on this model we can define what a ”100-year
flood” is - this is a flood level expected to be exceeded on average once every 100 years. This is then used
for infrastructure planning (dams, flood control systems, insurance companies calculate premiums etc. )

Contour plots of a multinormal distribution display the regions where the density is constant. In the
bivariate case, these iso-density curves are ellipses centered at the mean. Their shape and orientation are
determined by the covariance matrix, with the eigenvalues indicating the spread in each direction and the
eigenvectors indicating the axes of the ellipses. In higher dimensions, these contours become ellipsoids.
Their orientation and shape are determined by the covariance matrix: The center of the ellipses is the
mean μ. The axes of the ellipses align with the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix Σ.The lengths of the
semi-axes are related to the square roots of the eigenvalues of Σ. these contour plots visually represent
how the density ”spreads out” in different directions and how the correlation between variables affects the
shape of the distribution.

If the variables are only uncorrelated (i.e. the correlation ρ = 0) but have different variances, then the
covariance matrix is diagonal but not proportional to the identity. In that case, the iso-density contours
are ellipses with axes aligned with the coordinate axes, and their radii are proportional to the standard

9 Likelihood Function
The likelihood function is one of the most fundamental concepts in statistical inference. It quantifies
how probable the observed data are for different values of the unknown parameters. Unlike a probability
function, which expresses the probability of an event given a parameter, the likelihood function treats the
data as fixed and considers the parameter as a variable.
Likelihood-based methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), are widely used in param-
eter estimation, model selection, and Bayesian inference.

14.3 Conjugate Priors
A conjugate prior is a prior distribution that, when combined with a likelihood function (via Bayes’
theorem), produces a posterior distribution that is in the same family as the prior. In other words, if
you choose a conjugate prior for your likelihood, the mathematical form of the prior is preserved in the
posterior, simplifying the process of updating your beliefs with new data.

We will set α = 0.05.Suppose we have observed the following data: n=5 were asked about the model they
would buy, one of them chose model A, thus k=1. If the null hypothesis is true, i.e. p=0.1, we would
expect to see around 10 percent of the customers to buy model A. Given a sample of size 5, that is less than
1. We would like to find the probability that in such a sample size, we would observe 1 or more extreme

following
P(k ≥ 1|n = 5,p = 0.1) = 1 − P(k = 0|n = 5,p = 0.1) = 1 − 0.95 ≈ 0.41
(The significance probability, or p-value, is the chance of observing data that are as or more supportive of
the alternative hypothesis than the data that were collected, when the null hypothesis is true.) This value
is high, even more it is greater than 0.05. Thus, based on such a small sample, the null hypothesis can
not be rejected. If we had a large sample, we could perform the test for proportions. However, that is not
applicable here. What is important in this frequentist approach is that the test does not confirm the null
hypothesis. We just say that we do not have enough evidence to reject it. Thus, based on this sample, we
may decide that p=10%.

particular weekend is p. Compute the expected gain if you insure and if you do not. What is the best
course of action? Arrive at a decision.
